domain: The discredited doctrine of 'sumptuary law' — state regulation of what people may wear, eat, or spend on — and what was lost when liberal societies abandoned the idea that consumption could be a matter of public concern rather than private choice
topic: The discredited doctrine of 'sumptuary law' — state regulation of what people may wear, eat, or spend on — and what was lost when liberal societies abandoned the idea that consumption could be a matter of public concern rather than private choice

movement.gist: Introduce sumptuary law as a byword for pettiness and prejudice: medieval and early-modern statutes forbidding merchants' wives from wearing silk, peasants from wearing certain furs, the wrong classes from carrying certain colours — presented via the ridicule it now universally receives.

Steelman: sumptuary law was not really about fabric but about capping the ruinous, self-escalating arms race of status display — a crude mechanism that nonetheless did the real work of limiting positional spending before markets and advertising made that arms race unlimited.

Name what mainstream liberal consumer culture lost by discrediting the whole apparatus: no successor institution exists to slow status-driven overconsumption, so the function sumptuary law performed (however badly) has simply vanished, leaving positional competition to run unchecked through markets alone.
Withhold endorsement explicitly — the historical laws were entangled with caste enforcement and cannot be revived or excused; the loss is real but the remedy is not resurrection.

primary.axis: individual consumer sovereignty vs. consumption as a legitimate object of collective governance
poles: the liberal view that what one buys and wears is nobody's business but one's own
the sumptuary tradition's claim that visible consumption structures social relations and therefore is everybody's business

secondary.axis: the historical form of sumptuary law (class-marking, moralistic, often xenophobic) vs. the abstract regulatory function it performed (status-signalling restraint)
poles: sumptuary law as snobbish class enforcement, rightly abolished
sumptuary law as a crude but functioning brake on positional competition, wrongly abolished along with its ugliness

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension supplies the steelman's material — separating the odious mechanism from the useful function is what lets the essay affirm the function's loss without reviving the mechanism

family_realization.note: Paragraph one ridicules sumptuary laws; paragraph two reverses this by steelmanning their 'clumsy referee' function. The endorsement trap—'were they good?'—is expertly dodged by 'We were right to burn the instrument. We simply had nothing else.' Difficulty precisely realized.

ending_behavior.note: Final sentence narrows aperture sharply: 'We were right to burn the instrument. We simply had nothing else that did the work, and we still have nothing.' One flat verdict; cost explicit; closure costed rather than resolved.

voice_consistency.note: Genial contrarian throughout: 'Was there ever a law so easy to laugh at?' (concedes before striking). Concrete particular: Florentine lady arguing buttons lack buttonholes. One moment of uneven polish: 'Nor, for what it is worth, do I.' Mostly epigrammatic but not formulaic.

distractor_efficiency.note: Q1(A): scope_inflation—Hirsch illustrates but passage never narrates replacement. Q2(B): adjacent—author explicitly rejects salvage. Q3(D): categorical clarity trap—passage attributes collapse to ideology, not enforcement clarity. Q4(D): half-truth—author proposes no magistrate. Q5(A): adjacent—complicates motive, not function thesis. Q6(B): stage_misattribution—restoration, not loss. Q7(A): stance_misread—author's own claim. Most traps genuine.

explanation_quality.note: Every wrong option tied to specific passage location and mechanism: scope drift, adjacent answers, half-truths from single paragraph, misread stance. Never generic 'not mentioned.' 'Category_slip' and 'stage_misattribution' name real cognitive traps. No lazy extremity dismissals.

answers.reasoning: Passage traces loss of restraining function after rightful abolition of sumptuary laws.
Directly stated: stated reasons nonsense, effect was ceiling on neighbour-driven spending.
Passage never says enforcement failed due to inability to distinguish cloth types.
Dinner party models escalating positional game that sumptuary law referees interrupted.
If informal conventions still cap display, the claimed total loss/absence is complicated.
Mirrors abolition of restraint causing unchosen escalating spending, matching author's thesis.
Author counters 'no genuine loss' view with 'the loss is real'; presents but rejects it.
No institution inherited the function supports claim that abolition left true absence, unaddressed.
